# Wearing Red: Women Unite to Raise Heart Disease Awareness

(CNN) -- Anita Dunham's first heart attack announced itself through an inexplicable pain radiating through her arm, followed by a sudden, terrifying breathlessness. She was only 34 at the time. As she dressed that morning, the pain in her chest and arms grew so intense that she could barely speak.

Jolen Johnson captured this moment on camera, photographing co-workers dressed in red on Friday in Cedar Park, Texas. Dunham, who survived a second heart attack in 2002, donned red that day to help raise awareness about heart disease. Now 64, she hopes to spread a vital message to women everywhere: heart disease—the leading cause of death among women—does not discriminate, striking women from every background and walk of life. She and others shared their personal stories with CNN's iReport.com. *Read more about Dunham.*

The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, a division of the National Institutes of Health, sponsored this Wear Red initiative to underscore a powerful truth, as stated on its website: "Heart Disease Doesn't Care What You Wear—It's the #1 Killer of Women."

For many participants, the choice to wear red carried deeply personal weight, rooted in the loss of loved ones to this disease. Robin Savage, 42, of San Juan Capistrano, California, explained that heart disease had touched three generations of her family—her grandfather, father, and mother all suffered from it. Beyond wearing red herself, she actively documents heart health events for a local website. *See more from iReporters on National Wear Red Day »*

Savage herself relies on beta blockers to manage a heart that occasionally races after consuming certain foods, particularly those containing the preservative MSG. She maintains a vigilant approach to her diet and commits to 30 minutes of daily exercise to safeguard her health. *iReport.com: Heart Disease runs in my family.*

Though she carefully monitors the diets of her two sons, ages 9 and 12, Savage harbors a quiet fear—that she might not live to see them grow into adulthood. "It's such a huge void in your life," she reflected, "especially when you have your own kids and you don't have your mom around to, say, ask questions. I was completely lost when I had kids." *Visit CNNhealth.com, your connection to better living.*

Peggy Roesch, a 24-year-old graphic designer from Cincinnati, Ohio, recounted how her grandfather's heart attack five years ago left a lasting impression. More recently, she found inspiration in her marathon-running mother, which motivated her to take up running herself. *iReport.com: Seeing red.*

In West Palm Beach, Florida, Eileen Velez has rallied her co-workers to wear red in solidarity every year since 2007. "If everyone is wearing red at the same time," she noted, "somebody is going to notice." *iReport.com: Kimley-Horn and Associates.*

Yet despite this growing nationwide movement, Dunham observed that she saw no evidence of similar participation in her hometown of Earlimart, California, that Friday. Still, her message to those at risk remains clear and urgent: watch your weight. "I tell [my daughter] every day," she said, "'You know you need to start watching your diet or you're going to be in the hospital with a heart attack.'"

*CNN's Cristina Martin contributed to this report.*

# Wearing Red for a Reason: Women Unite Against Heart Disease

Anita Dunham was only 34 years old when her world changed in an instant. What began as mysterious, unexplained pain in her arm quickly escalated into difficulty breathing—symptoms she never imagined could signal a heart attack at such a young age. That harrowing experience marked the beginning of a lifelong battle with heart disease, one that would resurface nearly two decades later when she suffered a second heart attack in 2002.

Now 64 years old, Dunham has transformed her personal health crisis into a mission of awareness. This past Friday, she joined countless others across the country in wearing red, a simple yet powerful gesture aimed at reminding people that heart disease remains the number one killer of women. Her message is clear: heart disease does not discriminate. It can strike women from every background, age group, and walk of life—sometimes when they least expect it.

Dunham's efforts align with a larger national campaign led by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, which has long championed National Wear Red Day. The initiative serves as an annual call to action, urging communities to recognize that heart disease poses a serious threat to women everywhere, regardless of what they choose to wear on any given day. The red clothing serves as a visual reminder and conversation starter, sparking discussions about prevention, symptoms, and the importance of taking women's heart health seriously.

Among those who have embraced this cause is Robin Savage, 42, whose connection to heart disease runs deep within her family history. Savage has watched heart disease affect three generations before her—her grandfather, her father, and her mother all struggled with the condition. This family legacy has made her acutely aware of her own vulnerability, prompting her not only to wear red each year but also to actively document heart health events, using her voice and platform to spread awareness to others who might not realize how genetics can play a role in cardiovascular risk.

For Savage, managing her own heart condition has become a daily reality. She relies on beta blockers to help regulate her heart function, while carefully monitoring her diet to minimize additional strain on her cardiovascular system. Yet beneath this disciplined routine lies a deeper, more emotional fear—the possibility that she might follow in her mother's footsteps and pass away at a young age, leaving her two sons to grow up without a parent, just as she once experienced with her own mother's early death.

Savage's story, much like Dunham's, underscores why campaigns like National Wear Red Day matter so much. Behind the statistics are real women facing real fears, fighting to protect not just their own lives, but the futures of the families who depend on them. Their willingness to share their stories serves as a powerful reminder that heart disease is not just a statistic—it's a deeply personal battle that touches families across generations, making awareness and early action more critical than ever.

# National Wear Red Day Sparks Wave of Personal Stories as Americans Unite Against Heart Disease

**By CNN Staff**

Across the country today, offices, schools, and communities turned into seas of crimson as Americans marked National Wear Red Day, an annual observance aimed at raising awareness about heart disease—the leading cause of death for women in the United States.

The day, which falls within American Heart Month, has become more than a fashion statement. On CNN's iReport platform, ordinary people have been submitting deeply personal accounts of survival, loss, and vigilance, transforming a symbolic gesture into a public archive of lived experience with a disease that kills nearly 400,000 women annually.

## Stories From the Heart

Among the submissions is that of a Ohio mother who described the moment she recognized the subtle warning signs of a heart attack in herself—fatigue, jaw discomfort, and a vague sense that something was wrong—symptoms she says she might have dismissed were it not for a public awareness campaign she'd seen the year before.

"I didn't have the classic chest-clutching moment you see in movies," she wrote in her iReport submission. "It was quieter than that. If I hadn't known to pay attention, I might not be here writing this."

Other iReporters shared stories of losing mothers, sisters, and grandmothers to a disease that experts say remains under-recognized in women, whose symptoms often differ from the textbook presentations more commonly associated with men.

A Texas nurse who submitted photos of her family wearing red described her own mother's death from heart disease at age 52. "She thought it was heartburn," the nurse wrote. "It took years for me to stop asking 'what if.' Now I tell everyone I know: don't wait, don't guess, get it checked."

## A Campaign Rooted in Data

The American Heart Association, which spearheads the Go Red for Women initiative alongside National Wear Red Day, notes that heart disease kills more women than all forms of cancer combined, yet public perception has historically lagged behind that statistic. Awareness campaigns over the past two decades are credited with helping to reverse decades-long increases in cardiovascular deaths among women, though officials caution that progress has plateaued in recent years amid rising rates of obesity, diabetes, and hypertension.

Health officials emphasize that risk factors—high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, poor diet, and physical inactivity—are often preventable or manageable, making public awareness a critical tool in reducing the disease's toll.

## Amplifying Voices Through Citizen Journalism

CNN's iReport section has long served as a space where audience members contribute directly to coverage of major events, and National Wear Red Day has proven to be a particularly resonant moment for that kind of participatory storytelling. Submissions this year included photographs of red-clad coworkers linking arms in solidarity, tributes to relatives lost to cardiac events, and calls to action encouraging viewers to learn CPR or schedule overdue checkups.

For many contributors, the platform offers something a hashtag alone cannot: an opportunity to memorialize loved ones and, they hope, to prompt someone else to take a warning sign seriously.

"If one person reads this and calls their doctor instead of shrugging it off," one iReporter wrote, "then it was worth sharing."

As the red-clad crowds disperse and the day draws to a close, health advocates say the true measure of the campaign's success won't be visible today—but in the lives it may help save down the road.

# Beyond the Pink Ribbon: Women Confront America's Leading Killer

*How family history and personal vigilance are reshaping the conversation around heart disease*

For years, breast cancer awareness campaigns have dominated women's health conversations, their pink ribbons ubiquitous every October. But health experts say there's a bigger threat to women that deserves equal attention: heart disease, which kills more women annually than all forms of cancer combined.

For women like Anita Dunham, that statistic isn't abstract—it's personal.

"My mother had her first heart attack at 52. My grandmother died of heart disease. When I turned 50, I stopped thinking of heart disease as something that happened to other people's families," says Dunham, a 54-year-old teacher from Ohio. "I started paying attention to symptoms I would have brushed off before—the fatigue, the mild chest tightness. Family history changed how I listen to my own body."

Dunham's experience reflects a broader awakening among women about cardiovascular risk. According to the American Heart Association, heart disease remains the leading cause of death for women in the United States, yet studies consistently show women underestimate their personal risk and often delay seeking care when symptoms arise.

## The Family History Factor

Genetics play a significant role in cardiovascular risk, and for many women, understanding their family's medical history has become a critical first step in prevention.

"I didn't take it seriously until I started asking questions at family gatherings," says Robin Savage, 47, who discovered that three of her father's siblings had experienced heart attacks before age 60. "Once I had that full picture, I brought it to my doctor. We started monitoring my cholesterol and blood pressure more aggressively than they might have otherwise."

Savage's proactive approach illustrates what cardiologists increasingly recommend: treating family health history as essential medical data, not just casual conversation.

"Women often know their family's cancer history intimately but have never asked about heart disease," says Dr. Elena Ramirez, a cardiologist who specializes in women's cardiovascular health. "A father's heart attack at 55, a grandmother's stroke—these are critical data points. I tell my patients: your family tree is a health document."

## Symptoms That Look Different

Part of the challenge in heart disease prevention for women lies in symptom recognition. Unlike the crushing chest pain often associated with heart attacks in men, women frequently experience subtler warning signs.

"Nobody told me that fatigue and nausea could be heart-related," Dunham reflects. "I thought heart attacks looked like what you see in movies—someone clutching their chest. My symptoms were so vague I almost didn't go to the ER."

Savage echoes this concern: "We need better education about what heart disease actually feels like for women. Jaw pain, shortness of breath, unusual tiredness—these don't scream 'heart attack' the way chest-clutching does on TV."

## Taking Control Through Prevention

Both women have transformed their family history knowledge into concrete lifestyle changes—incorporating regular cardiovascular exercise, adjusting diets to reduce sodium and processed foods, and scheduling consistent screenings for blood pressure and cholesterol.

"I used to think prevention meant occasionally eating a salad," Savage laughs. "Now I understand it means consistent monitoring, honest conversations with my doctor, and not ignoring small changes in how I feel."

Dr. Ramirez emphasizes that this kind of engaged, informed patient advocacy is exactly what can move the needle on women's heart health outcomes.

"Women who understand their family history and advocate for appropriate screening are catching problems earlier," she notes. "We're seeing better outcomes when patients come in already informed and asking specific questions."

## A Call for Broader Awareness

Both Dunham and Savage hope their stories encourage other women to have frank conversations with relatives about family medical history and to push past hesitancy in discussing heart health with their doctors.

"This isn't about living in fear," Dunham says. "It's about being informed enough to advocate for yourself. I want my daughters to know their grandmother's and great-grandmother's history so they're paying attention decades before I started."

As Savage puts it: "Heart disease prevention starts with a conversation—with your family, with your doctor, and honestly, with yourself about what risks you're willing to ignore."

---

*Women concerned about their cardiovascular risk are encouraged to discuss family history with both relatives and healthcare providers, and to learn more about heart disease symptoms specific to women through resources like the American Heart Association's Go Red for Women campaign.*

# Heart Disease: The Silent Threat Killing More Women Than All Cancers Combined

*By CNN Health*

---

Sarah Martinez was 42, ran marathons, and considered herself the picture of health. She never imagined that a persistent feeling of "just not right" would turn out to be a heart attack—one that nearly killed her.

"I kept thinking, 'Women my age don't have heart attacks,'" Martinez recalled from her home in Denver. "I was wrong. So wrong."

Martinez's story is far from unique. Heart disease remains the leading cause of death among American women, claiming approximately one in five female lives annually—more than all forms of cancer combined, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yet despite decades of awareness campaigns, experts say a dangerous knowledge gap persists.

## The Numbers Behind the Crisis

Cardiovascular disease kills roughly 300,000 women in the United States each year. Perhaps more alarming: studies show only about half of women recognize heart disease as their greatest health threat, according to the American Heart Association.

"We've made progress, but we're nowhere near where we need to be," said Dr. Nieca Goldberg, cardiologist and medical director at NYU Langone's Joan H. Tisch Center for Women's Health. "Women often present with different symptoms than men—fatigue, nausea, jaw pain, shortness of breath—and both patients and sometimes even doctors miss these warning signs."

## When Symptoms Don't Match Expectations

This symptom disparity nearly cost Martinez her life. Instead of the crushing chest pain often associated with heart attacks, she experienced overwhelming fatigue and mild discomfort between her shoulder blades for three days before finally seeking help.

"My husband wanted to take me to the ER immediately. I told him I probably just needed rest," she said. "That delay could have killed me."

Other survivors echo similar experiences. Denise Williams, a 55-year-old teacher from Atlanta, described her heart attack as feeling like "severe indigestion" rather than the dramatic chest-clutching moment portrayed in movies.

"I took antacids for two hours before my daughter insisted we go to the hospital," Williams said. "The doctor told me I was minutes away from a massive cardiac event."

## Awareness Campaigns Push for Change

In response to this ongoing crisis, the American Heart Association's "Go Red for Women" campaign—now in its third decade—continues expanding efforts to educate women about unique cardiac risk factors, including pregnancy complications, menopause-related changes, and autoimmune conditions that disproportionately affect women.

This February, hospitals nationwide participated in National Wear Red Day, with landmarks illuminated in red and community health screenings offered in underserved areas.

"Education saves lives," Goldberg emphasized. "When women understand their risk factors and recognize symptoms, they seek help faster. Time is muscle when it comes to heart attacks."

Public health officials are also targeting healthcare providers, pushing for updated training that addresses gender-specific presentations of heart disease and combats historical underdiagnosis in women, particularly Black and Hispanic women, who face even higher mortality rates.

## Life After Survival

Today, both Martinez and Williams have become advocates within their communities, sharing their stories at local health fairs and encouraging women to trust their instincts.

"If something feels wrong, don't wait," Martinez said. "Don't let anyone—including yourself—talk you out of getting checked."

Williams now leads a support group for female heart attack survivors. "We're rewriting the narrative," she said. "Heart disease isn't just an 'old man's disease.' It's happening to our mothers, sisters, daughters, and friends."

As awareness campaigns continue and research evolves, health experts stress that the most powerful tool remains simple: listening to your body and never dismissing symptoms, regardless of age or fitness level.

"Every woman needs to know her numbers—blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar," Goldberg said. "And every woman needs to know she's not immune."
